messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Phạm is a thirty-one-year-old Vietnamese American judge who has been married for three years and who, until recently, was regarded by his colleagues as one of the most composed and methodical people in his courthouse. He presented for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after surviving a catastrophic flash flood that struck the rural county where he had been attending a judicial conference. What began as an overcast afternoon deteriorated within hours into a wall of brown water that swept through the conference grounds, destroying two buildings and killing four attendees. Kiet had been trapped on the second floor of a partially collapsed structure for nearly six hours before emergency responders reached him. During that time he watched the water rise and recede, carrying debris and, at one point, the body of a colleague past the window where he clung to an interior doorframe. The air inside the building had taken on a thick, chemical smell from a ruptured cleaning supply closet somewhere below — a smell that mixed with mud and standing water into something he has never been able to name but has never forgotten.

In the weeks that followed, Kiet noticed that the memory did not behave the way he expected a memory to behave. It did not arrive as a coherent narrative. Instead it came in discrete, frozen images — the grey-green colour of the water at the window, the particular angle of a ceiling beam that had dropped to shoulder height, the colleague's red jacket moving past. Each image was a photograph rather than a film, and when any one of them surfaced it brought with it the full sensory weight of the original moment: the cold of the water he had waded through, the chemical smell, the vibration of the structure settling. He described these episodes to his intake clinician as feeling completely real, as though the room he was currently sitting in had simply ceased to exist. He was certain, during those moments, that something terrible was still happening.

The triggers that reliably produced these episodes became apparent to him gradually and with a kind of grim logic. An overcast sky with a particular heaviness to it — the specific grey of that afternoon — was enough. He began checking weather applications compulsively each morning, and on days that matched the meteorological signature of the flood he found reasons to remain in his chambers rather than travel between buildings. The sound of an ambulance siren passing the courthouse, or the antiseptic smell that drifted from the first-aid station located near the building's main entrance, produced the same effect. He began entering and exiting through a side door to avoid the first-aid station entirely, a habit his clerk noticed but did not comment on for several months.

Over time Kiet stopped going out beyond what his professional obligations strictly required. Evenings and weekends that had once included dinners with his wife's family, walks along the river near their neighbourhood, and occasional travel contracted into the apartment and the courthouse. He had come to believe, without quite articulating it to himself, that the world outside contained too many variables he could not control — weather that could shift, smells that could ambush him, sirens that could appear without warning. His wife, Linh, initially attributed his withdrawal to the demands of his caseload. By the eighth month she had stopped suggesting outings and had begun spending weekend afternoons at her sister's house instead, a change that registered to Kiet as evidence that something in their marriage had quietly altered.

He also worked hard not to think about the flood. He had developed a practice of immediately redirecting his attention whenever an image began to surface — reviewing case files, doing arithmetic in his head, turning on background noise. Rest itself had become something he avoided. Lying still in a quiet room felt, to him, like removing the last barrier between himself and the images, and so he had not genuinely relaxed in over a year. He stayed up late reading briefs, telling himself he was simply industrious.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a moment in open court. An ambulance passed on the street outside, its siren audible through the chamber windows, and he lost approximately thirty seconds — long enough that the court reporter looked up. He was most afraid that he was becoming unreliable. What he most hoped was that someone could explain to him why his own mind had stopped belonging to him.
